talks.title: Look at this Graph: Prioritizing Initial Access Threats & TTPS via Link Analysis | SLEUTHCON 2023
talks.teaser: See how links between threats and shared infection techniques can help defenders decide what to investigate first.
talks.summary: The speakers describe analyzing public reporting to rank initial access threats by their links to other threats and malware. They also map reported techniques for 26 threats, compare initial infection methods, and discuss how defenders can use those findings to prioritize detection work.

talks.title: Call Me Maybe? The Rise of Callback Phishing Emails | SLEUTHCON 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how callback phishing emails dodge traditional checks, and which sender, phone and image signals help catch them.
talks.summary:
Callback phishing is a form of trusted-brand impersonation. An email, often posing as a service such as PayPal, Norton or Coinbase, tries to get the recipient to phone a number, acting as an email-based version of classic cold-call tech scams. Detection is hard because these messages usually come from newly created free mail accounts, often Gmail, and contain no suspicious domain history or malicious link to inspect.

The talk covered common tactics: urgency about expiring services, rapidly rotated templates, VoIP callback numbers, and brand text embedded as images, which defeats simple keyword matching. Intended outcomes range from delivering malware or commercial remote-access tools to bank transfers and data theft. Useful signals include free-mail sender checks, email reputation, phone numbers (especially VoIP), OCR on image content, suspicious phrase or tone analysis, and whether the recipient has any prior contact with the sender. The speaker presented a detection logic that combines these signals and said they had not seen a single false positive from it.

A case study followed a call to one of these numbers. The caller had the target enter a verification code sent to the email address, then open a legitimate remote-support site and install its binary, after which a screen share began and a fake claim of compromise was shown. The speaker noted that scammers are adopting scam-baiting tactics and adding multi-factor steps to look credible. The takeaway for defenders is to layer sender, phone and image signals rather than rely on any single indicator.

talks.title: Exploring Initial Access Methods of Surprisingly Competent Government Employees | SLEUTHCON 2023
talks.teaser: Tracks a North Korean crypto-targeting group's newer initial access chains, from macOS scriptlets to OneNote lures.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a North Korean state-linked group the speaker tracks as TA-444, which Microsoft calls Sapphire Sleet, and its role in stealing cryptocurrency. The speaker cites chain analysis figures for recent crypto heists and a report that the group's proceeds help fund the country's nuclear missile program. Over the past year the group has cast a wider net, reaching smaller cryptocurrency firms with friendly email openers rather than relying only on social networks.

The middle section walks through several newer infection chains. A first macOS intrusion starts with an AppleScript file that beacons to a command server and retrieves an app that decrypts a PDF lure and a second stage. A Windows chain with nearly identical logic shares the same server on the same day, which suggested two separate software sets. In February, a registry file weakened security settings and a proxy configuration file routed traffic through a chosen port. A OneNote document carried an embedded MSI that dropped a first-stage backdoor called curl agent, and its contents varied by architecture. A December lure posing as a OneNote or OneDrive invoice led to a customized phishing page, and the speaker was unsure whether the group itself was behind it.

For defenders, the speaker argues detection is achievable because of the group's recognizable network protocol structures and its reliance on mshta and wscript after landing. Crypto businesses should not assume they are too small to be targeted. The speaker notes that the activity map is getting harder to draw cleanly, and the talk closes with that as an open question.

talks.title: Certified Bad: One malware, Two years of Certificates. | SLEUTHCON 2023
talks.teaser: Follows one malware operator's code-signing certificates over two years and the many unrelated families they signed.
talks.summary:
The talk explains Authenticode code signing certificates, which vouch for a developer's program and carry a hash to detect tampering. Extended validation certificates add stronger checks, and malware authors want them because Microsoft's SmartScreen trusts them. Impersonating a real organization is a common way to obtain one.

The case study follows Solar Marker, a modular malware family active since 2020. Over two years the speaker revoked about 50 certificates each week while the actor obtained replacements. Roughly 700 signed binaries pulled from VirusTotal were linked to them, and 14 other malware families shared the same certificates, including Zloader, IcedID and Cobalt Strike. Most certificates were abused within 50 days of issuance, often in the first week, suggesting they were stolen and not revoked. One certificate used for JuiceLedger, reported by Sentinel Labs in 2022, kept signing other malware until it was revoked in January.

The speaker also argues that resale and revocation shape the market: revoking a certificate cuts an impostor's profit and raises costs for buyers. The takeaways are that third-party signing is a visible route for malware, and shared certificates link families that would otherwise look unrelated, which helps researchers and law enforcement trace money between actors.

talks.title: My 0ktapus Teacher: New Actors, New Problems | SLEUTHCON 2023
talks.teaser: Traces how overlapping ransomware and extortion clusters got tangled, and why naming and tracking them is hard.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes a 2022 investigation that began with a suspicious IP address and a domain tied to a ransomware group called Lapsus$. Over several weeks the team found that the activity was far from uniform. Some actors used stolen credentials or Microsoft 365 session tokens, some stole data without extortion, and others ran aggressive direct extortion of executives and employees. Another cluster carried out SMS phishing against lookalike single sign-on pages and ultimately sold SIM swapping services. Public names from other vendors, including Octopus and Scattered Spider, added to the confusion, and some of the domains reported by one vendor overlapped with clusters the team was already tracking.

The middle of the talk covers the return of a former Lapsus$ member who operated under a new persona. The team could not link this person to the original group through technical evidence, so they relied on less reliable material such as Telegram activity and placed the operator in a subgroup named after a person. The speaker explains that the team's clustering method works well when technical data supports a link, but breaks down when personas and chat channels are the main evidence. Every group in their internal tracking must carry a numbered designation, while public names can still be used when describing it.

The closing section argues that the industry may need to rethink how it clusters cybercrime and how it communicates overlaps to clients. In the Q&A the speaker said the team had not formally changed its approach yet but was discussing ways to show relationships between groups. His advice to analysts is to keep customer-facing messages as simple as possible, because clients care more about what the activity means for them than about a full web of names.

talks.title: BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - 0 to 2^32 in 6 Minutes: Hunting Threats at Scale
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - 0 to 2^32 in 6 Minutes: Hunting Threats at Scale.
talks.summary: A long-running internet scanner recounts chasing a mythical 24-minute full-IPv4 scan, arguing speed matters less than what you probe and how you fingerprint responses. He hunts malware C2 and commoditized panels by tailoring follow-up requests—pulling full Cobalt Strike Beacon payloads, clustering watermarks, spawn-to processes, and staging quirks, and citing Conti leak IPs that matched default configurations. The talk extends to scanning Awkward Rain and RedLine-style stealers via panel-specific paths, urges defenders to scale hunting the way operators scale phishing, and invites attendees to spot his post-talk scans via a changed User-Agent as a light CTF.

talks.title: BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - These crypters have everything: An argument for caring about cry...
talks.teaser: Argues that crypters hiding malware deserve tracking, and shows detection ideas for two common examples.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that crypters, the tools adversaries use to encrypt, pack and load malicious code, deserve more attention from cyber crime researchers. The speaker explains that a crypter helps a payload slip past antivirus, and that antivirus alone misses much of what attackers do, so endpoint telemetry from tools such as Sysmon or Velociraptor is needed.

Two common crypters are walked through. CipherIt wraps its payload in AutoIt, a legitimate scripting language, so a renamed AutoIt binary is a masquerading signal, and certain command strings such as timeout commands also stand out in endpoint data. Pure Crypter works in stages: its loader downloads more code, waits using a PowerShell sleep command, injects its code into a newly spawned process, and then removes its own executable. Detection ideas here include encoded PowerShell, the sleep delay, and attempts to add Windows Defender exclusions.

The central point is to separate the crypter from the payload. Adversaries reuse the same crypter across families such as Redline, Raccoon and CryptBot, so detecting a crypter can flag many different threats at once. The speaker closes by calling on the community to publish more research on crypters, since few write-ups cover them.

talks.title: BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - Lions, Tigers, and Infostealers - Oh my!
talks.teaser: Explains how infostealer businesses sell stolen credentials to access brokers, and how those logins enable enterprise intrusions.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that infostealers, once a personal risk to individuals, have become an enterprise problem because they now supply the initial access used by a new class of attackers. The speaker walks through the infostealer business model: developers run the malware and its command infrastructure, sell builders to franchisees, and those franchisees run their own distribution campaigns. Their logs are then monetised through Telegram channels or credential marketplaces such as Russian Market and Genesis Market, and end buyers purchase the access. Advertised prices for panel access and subscriptions were shown as examples.

Using a screenshot-based example, the speaker links a log file naming pattern to purchases made on a marketplace. Actors in this space have different motivations, including extortion, ransomware, crypto theft and SIM swapping as a service, but they share tactics. These include starting from purchased credentials or tokens, targeting help desk, IT service providers or telcos to reach a final victim, and MFA fatigue. The case of the actor tracked as Dev 537 covered insider recruitment, identity compromise through business partners, privilege escalation by finding scripts with privileged credentials, and destructive actions once the victim was locked out.

For defenders, the main takeaways are that credential hygiene and session token lifetimes matter as much as malware removal, and that unmanaged personal devices and browser password syncing sit outside corporate visibility. The speaker recommends phishing-resistant MFA, disabling legacy authentication methods such as phone calls and push, and checking whether federation services like ADFS can be forced into weaker authentication.

talks.title: BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - Crimeware: Cooler Than APT?
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of BRUNCHCON 2022 (now SLEUTHCON) - Crimeware: Cooler Than APT?.
talks.summary: Sherry de Grippo delivers a provocative Sleuthcon/BRUNCHCON session arguing crimeware ecosystems deserve equal research attention to APTs, framed as humor to recruit analysts toward a new crimes-focused conference track. She recounts eighteen years spanning government, vendor, and intel roles, jokes about paying researchers, and disclaims that the pro-crimeware stance is rhetorical—not a real preference over nation-state work.
